summary: Describes how a small subset of SIP specifications can be used for presence, messaging and audio or video communication, by using only SIP's rendezvous and session initiation and avoiding emulation of older phone networks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: SIP has a huge toolbox. This says you need only a few tools to make simple calls and chats work.

questions: minimal sip for im and presence
how many sip standards do you need
subtitle: How to use a minimal subset of SIP for real-time web communications

tldr.problem: SIP is a powerful protocol for real-time communications, but supporting all its features requires implementing around 100 standards, which adds unnecessary complexity when building simple presence, messaging and voice or video applications on the web.
tldr.mechanism: This document describes how to accomplish presence, instant messaging, voice and video using only about 11 core SIP standards, by placing intelligence in the endpoints rather than in network servers and avoiding the emulation of legacy telephone features.
tldr.outcome: Simple SIP reduces implementation burden for web developers and enables SIP-based communications to be easily combined with rich web applications, though it is less suitable for complex enterprise telephone systems.

today: RFC 5638 is an Informational document published in September 2009. It helped establish the concept of "Simple SIP" for web-based applications and was cited in subsequent IETF work on SIP simplification. The rise of WebRTC has provided alternative approaches to web-based real-time communications, but simple SIP remains a valid approach for applications that need SIP interoperability with traditional systems.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is the Internet standard for real-time multimedia communications, widely used by both service providers and enterprises. However, SIP's complexity has grown over time as it accumulated features to support legacy telephone network models. Meanwhile, the web has evolved into a platform for rich Internet applications (RIAs) with powerful browsers and desktop clients that can handle application logic themselves. This document proposes an alternative: use SIP only for its core functions of rendezvous (finding people) and session initiation, while delegating complex features to the endpoints or to application gateways that serve traditional telephone networks. By doing so, the number of SIP standards needed drops from roughly 100 to about 11, making it feasible for web developers to implement SIP-based communications without mastering telephony concepts.
sections.eli5: SIP is complicated because it tries to act like a telephone network. But if you're building web apps where computers are smart, you can use just the simple parts and skip all the telephone stuff.

sections.title: The Endpoint in Web and SIP Architectures
sections.content: SIP was designed around a trapezoid model where two service provider networks each have outgoing and incoming proxy servers. However, SIP is equally valid as a peer-to-peer protocol without servers, and can be combined with web technologies. The key insight is that modern endpoints (PCs, smart phones, servers) can execute application logic directly, rather than requiring central network servers to manage features. In contrast to telephone networks where intelligence is centralized, the web architecture puts logic in the browser or client, allowing loose coupling of services and flexibility in how users configure their applications. For simple SIP, this means endpoints run the full presence, messaging, voice and video logic themselves, using the SIP proxy only for finding and contacting other endpoints. The document proposes that telephone network gateways be treated as special SIP endpoints that can translate between simple SIP on the internet side and complex telephone features on the PSTN side, rather than forcing simple SIP clients to understand telephone complexity.
sections.eli5: Instead of putting all the smart logic in the telephone network, let the computer or phone in your hand be smart. SIP then just helps your computer find and call someone else's computer.

sections.title: What Simple SIP Can and Cannot Accomplish
sections.content:
Simple SIP can establish one-to-one real-time multimedia sessions for presence, instant messaging, voice and video, and handle point-to-point and some conference applications. It can support security with authentication and encryption of media and signaling. It can integrate with rich web applications, allowing presence to be tied to web services and messaging to be combined with other data. Where SIP endpoints have access to geographic location and medical or emergency systems, powerful emergency applications become possible without PSAP (Public Safety Access Point) infrastructure.

What simple SIP cannot do well includes supporting legacy telephony features like emulating phone switches or managing complex numbering plans, supporting the PSTN-specific features the document lists out of scope, and handling long chains of SIP proxies and feature servers that are typical of VoIP networks built to mirror telephone architecture. The document clarifies borderline cases: PRACK (Provisional Response Acknowledgements) is primarily for multi-hop server networks and multi-hop PSTN interworking, so it is not needed for simple SIP; Non-Invite transaction handling (RFC 4320) may be needed on the Internet but is optional. The dividing line is clear when SIP is used on the Internet without intermediaries designed to support closed VoIP networks.
sections.eli5: Simple SIP handles calls, chats, presence and video between two people or in a group. It struggles with telephone company features like complex phone numbers or routing through many servers.

sections.title: The 11 Core SIP Standards
sections.content:
The document identifies the minimal set of mandatory references to implement simple SIP:

RFC 3261 is the core specification, defining SIP session establishment and the use of proxies and registrars. RFC 4566 defines SDP (Session Description Protocol), the standard format for describing media parameters, codecs and transport addresses. RFC 3264 specifies the offer/answer model for negotiating common media between two endpoints. RFC 3840 allows endpoints to advertise their capabilities (presence, IM, audio, video, fixed/mobile device type) so applications can disable features the far end does not support. RFC 3263 specifies how to locate SIP servers using DNS, with NAPTR, SRV and A record lookups. RFC 3265 provides an extensible framework for event notifications, used by presence. RFC 3856 defines presence as a SIP event, using SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY methods. RFC 3863 defines PIDF (Presence Information Data Format), the XML format for carrying presence. RFC 3428 defines the MESSAGE method for instant messaging in a pager model. RFC 4474 provides identity authentication using digital signatures in SIP requests. RFC 3581 defines the rport extension for symmetric response routing, helpful for NAT traversal.
sections.eli5: The 11 standards cover: basic SIP, describing media, negotiating what both sides support, finding SIP servers, event notifications, presence, instant messages, and identity verification.

sections.title: SIP Applications in Endpoints
sections.content: Simple SIP endpoints can accomplish most telephony functions by running the logic locally rather than relying on network features. The document cites examples from IETF work on SIP call control, including features like conference calls, hold and resume, call transfer and call waiting. Examples of endpoint-based features include integration with web services (a customer service agent speaking with a customer can invoke a web-based configuration tool or help portal), social network integration (presence tied to social networks, video calls launched from contact lists), and multimedia scenarios (watching an event on the web while discussing it with others via SIP video). The document emphasizes that SIP applications in endpoints can support a mix of real-time communications with rich web applications, offering flexibility that traditional telephone network features cannot provide. For instance, an emergency call application could include location information, vital signs monitoring, video consultation and self-help instructions, all beyond what telephone networks support.
sections.eli5: When the computer is smart, it can do lots of clever things: mix a video call with a web page, tie presence to your social network, or build new features without changing servers.
